result:
Before I write it up, there's one thing I haven't asked: why the museum wants this.

The answer shapes decisions you'd otherwise never see me make. It decides whether visitors need to install anything or just tap and listen. It decides how much the guide has to work on a weak signal in the galleries. It decides whether you'd want to know which stories people actually play, and how polished the volunteer upload needs to be. I'd rather make those calls the way you would than guess.

On what you'll get: the guide has several separate parts that each need to work before the next makes sense. Those are the volunteer upload, the automatic clean-up, the player with its language memory, and the codes beside the exhibits. None of it exists yet. So instead of one large design document, I'll set it out as a short staged plan: what gets built first, and what each stage gives you. Each stage's details get settled when we reach it. The decisions we've already made go in as you made them: remembering the visitor's language, and cleaning up recordings automatically.

So, in your own words: what's prompting the audio guide now, and what would tell you, a year in, that it's working?
